chapter_title: Implementing Actions with the New Input System

screens.title: Implementing Actions with the New Input System
screens.subtitle: Integrate your PlayerControls asset into C# using event-driven callbacks and sensible Action Map management.

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how to make your game respond to player input by wiring a generated Input Action Asset into C# scripts. We'll focus on the two interaction styles the Input System supports: event-driven callbacks, which fire methods when an action occurs, and polling, which reads the current input state on demand. You will see how Unity generates a typed class for your asset, how to instantiate that class, and how to subscribe to action events such as started, performed, and canceled. We will also practice reading input data from the InputAction. CallbackContext so you can obtain Vector2 movement or numeric button values safely. Finally, you will learn practical rules for enabling and disabling Action Maps to avoid conflicts between gameplay and UI. This matters because clean input handling reduces bugs, prevents accidental input conflicts and keeps your Update loop efficient. By the end you will have a working PlayerController pattern for movement and jumping that follows best practices and is easy to extend.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use the generated Input Action class and event callbacks for responsive, efficient input handling; enable only the Action Maps you need.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will write C# scripts that interact with a generated Input Action Asset, and you will know when to use event-driven callbacks versus polling. You will practice instantiating the PlayerControls class, subscribing to action events, and reading input values through the InputAction. CallbackContext. You will also implement player movement and a jump action using the recommended patterns that separate input reading from physics updates. Finally, you'll gain skills to manage multiple Action Maps and switch them dynamically so UI and gameplay inputs do not conflict. These objectives matter because handling input cleanly prevents bugs like movement while menus are open, and it keeps performance healthy by avoiding unnecessary polling. A short mnemonic: Instantiate → Subscribe → Read → Enable, which maps to creating the asset instance, registering callbacks, retrieving values, and enabling the appropriate action map at runtime.

screens.title: Skills to practice
screens.subtitle: Practical tasks and mental models you will build

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on actionable skills: wiring up Move and Jump, reading values correctly for physics, and toggling Action Maps during UI transitions. You will practice using lambda subscriptions for concise move handling and a dedicated method for jump logic so you can inspect the CallbackContext if needed. You will also learn when to use FixedUpdate for physics movement driven by a stored Vector2 and why AddForce should be used inside a controlled jump method with grounding checks. Finally you will practice polling only when necessary, for example detecting if a fire button is held for continuous effects. These abilities let you move from prototype input code toward production-grade, maintainable systems that avoid duplicated responsibility and keep input logic centralized. As you practice, watch for the common misconception that polling is always simpler; polling increases overhead and can hide event timing details crucial for crisp gameplay.

screens.title: Event-driven callbacks vs Polling
screens.subtitle: When to subscribe to actions and when to read values in Update

narration.text: First, make a clear distinction between event-driven callbacks and polling. Event-driven callbacks fire when the Input System detects that an action reaches a relevant phase, such as started, performed, or canceled. Subscribing to those events means your code runs only when something meaningful happens. This is efficient for discrete actions like jump presses, ability triggers, and menu selections. Polling, by contrast, asks the action for its current state each frame. Polling is useful when you need to know whether a button is currently held, or to continuously sample an analog control for procedural animation or sustained fire. A concrete example: for a jump you should subscribe to Jump. performed and trigger AddForce once. For a sprint mechanic that requires holding a button, you might poll IsPressed inside Update so you can apply speed while the button remains held. A common misconception is that polling always makes logic simpler; in many cases it introduces redundant checks and can blur the timing of discrete events. As a takeaway, prefer event-driven callbacks for discrete interactions and use polling only when continuous state matters, such as holding to run or charging an ability.

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: Use events for discrete actions, poll when you need continuous state like holding or charging.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Event vs Polling
Event-driven callbacks
Subscribe to action events and let the system call your handlers when input occurs.
Good for:
Discrete interactions like jump, interact, or primary attack triggers.
Example
playerControls.Gameplay.Jump.performed += OnJump;
Misconception
Not suitable for continuous hold checks without additional state tracking.
Polling
Read the current action state inside Update or FixedUpdate when you need continuous information.
Good for:
Holding to run, continuous firing, or sampling analog sticks every frame.
Example
if (playerControls.Gameplay.Fire.IsPressed()) { /* continuous fire */ }
Misconception
Polling always costs more, but when used sparingly it's appropriate for continuous effects.
Key Takeaway

Prefer events for single triggers and polling for sustained input; choose the pattern that makes intent and timing clear.

Check your understanding
Which approach would you use for a charged attack that starts on press and builds while held?
Pro tip
Combine: use performed to detect start, then poll a flag while the button is held to apply continuous charge.

screens.title: Using the generated PlayerControls class
screens.subtitle: Instantiate the asset class and expose action maps and actions

narration.text: Unity generates a typed C# class from your Input Action Asset, commonly named after the asset such as PlayerControls. This class gives you strongly-typed access to action maps and individual actions, so you'll write less string-based plumbing and get clearer code. In C# you typically create a private instance field, instantiate it in Awake or constructor, and then use that instance to subscribe to events or read values. For example, in Awake you might call new PlayerControls() and cache references. Remember to call Enable on the relevant action map in OnEnable and Disable in OnDisable so the map is active only when appropriate. A common mistake is to instantiate inside Update or to forget to enable the map, which either creates repeated instances or leaves the actions inactive. A concrete example appears in the provided PlayerController snippet: Awake constructs PlayerControls and sets up callbacks, OnEnable calls Gameplay. Enable, and OnDisable calls Gameplay. Disable. As a practical takeaway, keep the generated instance as a long-lived field on the component and manage its lifecycle in Awake/OnEnable/OnDisable to avoid object churn and unexpected inactive actions.

keyIdea.title: Instantiation pattern
keyIdea.text: Create the PlayerControls instance in Awake, enable maps in OnEnable, and disable them in OnDisable.

Pattern overview
Hold one instance per component, construct early, enable maps when the component becomes active, and disable when it stops.
Awake
playerControls = new PlayerControls();
OnEnable
playerControls.Gameplay.Enable();
OnDisable
playerControls.Gameplay.Disable();

// Awake
playerControls = new PlayerControls();
// OnEnable
playerControls.Gameplay.Enable();
// OnDisable
playerControls.Gameplay.Disable();
Common mistake

Instantiating inside Update or leaving maps enabled across contexts leads to duplicates or unintended input handling.

screens.title: Subscribing to action events
screens.subtitle: Use performed, started, and canceled to respond to input phases

narration.text: Subscribing to action events is the core of event-driven input. Each action exposes phases: started when the input begins, performed when the binding conditions are satisfied, and canceled when the input ends. For example, a press-and-release button may start when pressed, perform on press depending on interaction settings, and cancel on release. You usually subscribe in Awake or when you create the instance, and use OnEnable/OnDisable to control map activation. For movement, use Move. performed to capture Vector2 and Move. canceled to zero your stored input when the stick or keys return to neutral. For jump, subscribe to Jump. performed and call a dedicated handler that applies AddForce. A practical subscription pattern uses a lambda for short value capture: playerControls. Gameplay. Move. performed += ctx => currentMovementInput = ctx. ReadValue (); and a named method for jump: playerControls. Gameplay. Jump. performed += OnJump; This balances brevity and debuggability. A common trap is forgetting to unsubscribe on object destruction; while many patterns rely on disabling maps, explicitly removing handlers in OnDisable or OnDestroy prevents hidden references in complex lifecycles. The key takeaway: wire each phase you need, read values when available, and clean up to avoid dangling callbacks.

keyIdea.title: Subscription rules
keyIdea.text: Subscribe once during initialization, read values in handlers, and unsubscribe or disable maps to cleanly stop callbacks.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Subscribing to events
Event phases
Understand started, performed, and canceled so your logic runs at the right moment and you can track hold states.
Started
Triggered when the control first changes. Useful for starting animations or charging.
Performed
Fired when the action's interaction completes. Good for discrete triggers like jump.
Canceled
Fired when input ends. Useful to zero movement or stop charging.
Subscription pattern
// Move
playerControls.Gameplay.Move.performed += ctx => currentMovementInput = ctx.ReadValue();
playerControls.Gameplay.Move.canceled += ctx => currentMovementInput = Vector2.zero;
// Jump
playerControls.Gameplay.Jump.performed += OnJump;
Pro tip

Use lambdas for trivial captures and full methods when you need to inspect the CallbackContext or add diagnostics.

screens.title: InputAction.CallbackContext explained
screens.subtitle: What the context contains and how to read values safely

narration.text: InputAction. CallbackContext is the object your event handlers receive when an action fires. It encapsulates the state of the input event and provides helper methods to access the value and metadata. The two most commonly used members are ReadValue and phase checks. ReadValue is generic and returns the correct type when you specify one: ReadValue () for movement vectors or ReadValue () for analog triggers and buttons. The context also exposes the phase of the action so you can decide behavior based on whether the event is started, performed, or canceled. Another useful detail is that the context can indicate which device triggered the input, helpful when you need to adapt UI prompts or control hints. A concrete example: in a Move. performed handler you might call Vector2 moveInput = context. ReadValue (); and store that vector for physics movement. A common mistake is to call ReadValue with an incorrect type; this will not crash but will return a default that can confuse logic. As a takeaway, use the typed ReadValue calls that match your action control type and check the phase only when you need different behavior for start, perform, or cancel.

keyIdea.title: Context rule
keyIdea.text: Use context.ReadValue<T>() with the correct T matching the action's control type; phase tells you the event timing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › CallbackContext
What it provides
  • ReadValue() — Returns the input value typed to T, e.g., Vector2 for movement.
  • phase info — Know whether the event is started, performed, or canceled.
  • device metadata — Identify which device triggered the action if needed.
Examples
Vector2 moveInput = context.ReadValue<Vector2>(); float pressure = context.ReadValue<float>();
Key Takeaway

Match ReadValue's type to the action's expected control type and use phase checks for nuanced behavior.

screens.title: Movement handling: capture then apply
screens.subtitle: Store movement vectors from callbacks and move in FixedUpdate

narration.text: A reliable pattern for physics-based movement is to capture input in callbacks and then apply it in FixedUpdate. When Move. performed fires, read a Vector2 from the context and store it in a private Vector2 field. When Move. canceled fires, reset that stored vector to zero. In FixedUpdate, convert the stored Vector2 into a Vector3 movement and call Rigidbody. MovePosition or apply velocity so the physics system remains authoritative. The PlayerController example demonstrates this: the callback writes currentMovementInput, and FixedUpdate does rb. MovePosition(rb. position + movement). This separation avoids reading input and applying forces on different timing domains, which can cause jitter or inconsistent behavior. A common misconception is to call AddForce from the performed handler for each move event; this is incorrect because the callback frequency and physics frames differ. Instead, treat callbacks as intent setters and apply that intent each physics tick. For example, convert the Vector2 to world-space directions and multiply by moveSpeed and Time. fixedDeltaTime. The takeaway: use callbacks to record intent and FixedUpdate to execute physics deterministically. Movement handling: capture then apply means use callbacks to set input state and fixedupdate to apply movement via rigidbody for consistent physics behavior.. In practical terms, store movement vectors from callbacks and move in fixedupdate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Apply pattern
keyIdea.text: Use callbacks to set input state and FixedUpdate to apply movement via Rigidbody for consistent physics behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Movement handling
Capture intent
Subscribe to Move.performed and Move.canceled to set currentMovementInput.
// Move callbacks
playerControls.Gameplay.Move.performed += ctx => currentMovementInput = ctx.ReadValue();
playerControls.Gameplay.Move.canceled += ctx => currentMovementInput = Vector2.zero;
Apply in FixedUpdate
Convert to Vector3 and use MovePosition to keep movement in the physics step.
void FixedUpdate() {
 Vector3 movement = new Vector3(currentMovementInput.x, 0, currentMovementInput.y) * moveSpeed * Time.fixedDeltaTime;
 rb.MovePosition(rb.position + movement);
}
Key Takeaway

Separate intent capture from physics application to avoid jitter and inconsistent input timing.

screens.title: Implementing Jump with CallbackContext
screens.subtitle: Subscribe to Jump.performed and apply AddForce with a grounding check

narration.text: Jump behavior is an archetypal example of a discrete input action. The Input System should trigger your jump logic when Jump. performed fires. In your OnJump handler you receive an InputAction. CallbackContext; you can call context. ReadValue () for pressure-sensitive jumps, but for a simple button press you often just act when performed is received. Before applying AddForce, check that the player is grounded to avoid double jumps unless the design allows them. The PlayerController example calls rb. AddForce(Vector3. up * jumpForce, ForceMode. Impulse) inside OnJump. A concrete scenario: when spacebar is pressed on keyboard or the A button on a gamepad, Jump. performed will call OnJump, which checks a grounded boolean and then applies impulse. A common mistake is to perform camera or animation-sensitive logic directly in the jump callback without coordinating with physics; instead, apply physics impulses and then trigger animations based on the resulting state to keep things consistent. The key practice is: subscribe to Jump. performed, check grounded state, apply AddForce, and optionally log or trigger animation events after physics is applied. Implementing Jump with CallbackContext means trigger jump on performed, validate grounded state, and apply addforce in the handler safely.. In practical terms, subscribe to jump.performed and apply addforce with a grounding check. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Jump rule
keyIdea.text: Trigger jump on performed, validate grounded state, and apply AddForce in the handler safely.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Jump implementation
OnJump handler
Use Jump.performed to run jump logic and avoid using per-frame polling for a single press.
void OnJump(InputAction.CallbackContext context) {
 if (!isGrounded) return;
 rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
 Debug.Log("Jump performed!");
}
Grounding & animation
Validate grounded state before impulse and then update animation state after physics to keep visuals consistent.
Common mistake
Applying AddForce without grounding checks results in unintended double jumps.
Scenario
Spacebar or gamepad A triggers Jump.performed and runs the handler once per press.

screens.title: Polling techniques and IsPressed
screens.subtitle: When to use IsPressed and ReadValue in Update or FixedUpdate

narration.text: Polling has its place. Use it when you need continuous information about an input's current state. The Input System offers convenience methods like IsPressed to check whether an action is currently active, and ReadValue to sample analog values. For example, a weapon that fires repeatedly while the fire button is held can rely on IsPressed inside Update to gate repeated shots. Another scenario is a run toggle that increases move speed while a specific button remains depressed. When polling in Update, combine it with timing or cooldown logic to avoid firing every frame. If the polled state affects physics, sample in FixedUpdate or translate the polled flag into a stored variable that physics code uses. A common trap is polling every action indiscriminately; this undoes the efficiency of event-driven callbacks and can make intent unclear. A practical recommendation: prefer events, but where continuous state is required — holding to run, charging an ability, or sustained fire — poll the action selectively and map that to clear state variables your game logic uses. This keeps polling targeted and maintainable. Polling techniques and IsPressed means poll only for continuous state such as holding; convert polled values into state variables for deterministic use in update or fixedupdate.. In practical terms, when to use ispressed and readvalue in update or fixedupdate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Polling guideline
keyIdea.text: Poll only for continuous state such as holding; convert polled values into state variables for deterministic use in Update or FixedUpdate.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Polling techniques
When to poll
Holding actions, continuous fire, or charging mechanics benefit from polling.
Example
if (playerControls.Gameplay.Fire.IsPressed()) { /* sustain fire */ }
Best practice
Sample in Update for input-only logic; for physics, set flags and apply in FixedUpdate.
Avoid over-polling
Polling every action defeats the performance and clarity benefits of event-driven code.
Check

Only poll when continuous state is required; otherwise prefer event callbacks.

screens.title: Managing multiple Action Maps
screens.subtitle: Enable and disable Gameplay and UI maps to control input context

narration.text: Action Maps let you group inputs by context. Typical games use a Gameplay map for movement and combat and a UI map for menu navigation. The recommended pattern is to enable only the map relevant to the current context. When play begins, call playerControls. Gameplay. Enable(). When the pause menu opens, call playerControls. Gameplay. Disable() and playerControls. UI. Enable(). This ensures the left stick doesn't both move the character and move a menu cursor. A common mistake is enabling all maps simultaneously; this causes conflicting responses to the same device input. If you have overlay UIs that should allow gameplay beneath, plan those exceptions carefully and consider selectively disabling only conflicting actions. Another important detail is lifecycle: enable and disable maps in OnEnable/OnDisable or on explicit UI open/close events so their activation state matches the visible game state. A practical example: on opening the pause screen, invoke Gameplay. Disable() and UI. Enable(); on closing, reverse the calls. The core benefit is predictable input handling that maps directly to the player's intent in each state. Managing multiple Action Maps means enable only the relevant action map for the player's current context to avoid conflicting inputs.. In practical terms, enable and disable gameplay and ui maps to control input context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Map management
keyIdea.text: Enable only the relevant Action Map for the player's current context to avoid conflicting inputs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Action Map Management
Typical maps
Design separate maps for Gameplay and UI to make responsibility explicit.
Gameplay
Movement, jump, combat actions.
UI
Menu navigation, submit/cancel for UI elements.
Switching example
// Open pause menu
playerControls.Gameplay.Disable();
playerControls.UI.Enable();
// Close pause menu
playerControls.UI.Disable();
playerControls.Gameplay.Enable();
Common mistake

Enabling both maps causes the same input to trigger multiple systems; enable only the map you need.

screens.title: Implement the PlayerController
screens.subtitle: Follow the lab to move the cube and trigger Jump using the PlayerControls asset

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through creating a Player GameObject, attaching a Rigidbody, and implementing the PlayerController script using the PlayerControls asset. First, create a cube and add a Rigidbody with rotations frozen so it won't tumble. Next, create the PlayerController script and instantiate the PlayerControls class in Awake. AddForce upward using jumpForce. Run the scene and test WASD or arrow keys and Spacebar or gamepad A. Watch the Console for the debug message to confirm Jump. performed fired. This exercise enforces the pattern: capture in callbacks, apply in physics, and manage maps. After testing, consider how you might add a Run action that engages while a button is held. Implement the PlayerController means create the player, attach rigidbody, instantiate playercontrols, subscribe to actions, enable maps, and apply movement in fixedupdate.. In practical terms, follow the lab to move the cube and trigger jump using the playercontrols asset. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Assessment & extension: Interact and pause handling
screens.subtitle: Test subscribing to Interact and toggling maps for the pause menu

narration.text: For assessment, implement two tasks that exercise the patterns you've learned. First, add an Interact action (Button) to your Gameplay map and subscribe to Interact. performed to trigger a door animation or interaction. The expected code pattern is to wire playerControls. Gameplay. Interact. performed += OnInteractPerformed in Awake, and define OnInteractPerformed that logs or triggers the interaction. The provided example in the chapter shows exactly this pattern. Second, implement a pause menu that demonstrates Action Map management: when the pause menu opens, call playerControls. Gameplay. Disable() and playerControls. UI. Enable(); when closing, reverse the calls. Test the common mistake by temporarily enabling both maps and observe how the same stick input drives both player movement and menu navigation — this will illustrate why map switching matters. As an extension, design a Run action that becomes active only while a specific button is held: you can either subscribe to started and canceled to flip a run flag, or poll IsPressed each frame and set running state accordingly. The assessment checks your ability to wire events, manage maps, and reason about discrete versus continuous input patterns.

narration.text: Let's summarize the critical concepts you should remember. First, prefer event-driven input for discrete actions: subscribe to performed, started, and canceled so your code runs only when relevant. Second, use InputAction. CallbackContext. ReadValue with the correct type to safely retrieve Vector2 and numeric values inside handlers. Third, separate input capture from physics: store intent in callbacks and apply movement in FixedUpdate using Rigidbody methods. Fourth, manage Action Maps by enabling only the map relevant to current context so inputs do not trigger multiple systems. These practices produce clearer, more maintainable input code and avoid common bugs like movement while a menu is open or accidental double-jumps. Keep these concepts in mind as you implement PlayerController and expand your control schemes. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact cards to keep handy

narration.text: A quick reference to keep beside your editor: first, instantiate PlayerControls in Awake and manage its lifecycle in OnEnable and OnDisable. Second, subscribe to performed for discrete events and use context. ReadValue with the correct type to access input data. Third, when implementing physics movement, capture input intent in callbacks and apply it in FixedUpdate to keep physics deterministic. Use Action Maps to separate responsibilities and only enable the map appropriate for the current UI or gameplay context. These three simple rules cover most practical cases you'll encounter while wiring input into gameplay features. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Quick Reference
Lifecycle
Instantiate in Awake; enable/disable maps in OnEnable/OnDisable.
Read Values
Use context.ReadValue<T> with the correct type for actions.
Apply Input
Capture intent in callbacks; apply movement in FixedUpdate.
Final takeaway

Follow event-driven patterns for clarity, use polling sparingly, and switch maps to keep input context explicit.

ai_generation_note: Create a 15-minute live coding video. Start with the `PlayerController` script from the previous chapter. Demonstrate how to instantiate the `PlayerControls` asset, subscribe to `Move` (using lambda expressions for `performed` and `canceled`) and `Jump` (using a dedicated `OnJump` method) actions. Show the `InputAction.CallbackContext` in action, reading `Vector2` for movement and triggering `AddForce` for jump. Include a split-screen view of the C# script and the Unity Editor playing the game, demonstrating the cube moving and jumping. Then, briefly explain how to manage multiple Action Maps by enabling/disabling them. End with a reflection prompt asking learners to consider how they would implement a "Run" action that only activates when a specific button is held down. Emphasize best practices for clean, event-driven code.
